w1.label: Warm-up, quick answers from the paper
items: What process did the authors follow to conduct this scoping review?
How did they arrive at their research question, and why did they ask about facilitators as well as barriers?
Of the 18 categories, which three do the authors name as the core considerations for trustworthy, adoption-centric AI?
What examples of bias problems does the paper give?

w1.label: Breakout rooms, each room picks one
items: The authors read every theme both ways, as a barrier and as a facilitator. Describe how they did this, and why they chose to.
The paper cites four reasons to make AI explainable: to justify, to control, to improve and to discover. Give one real or imagined example of each from your own field.
What does the paper suggest to fix bias problems? Which of these fixes would have caught the cost-as-a-proxy problem in the Obermeyer example?

w1.label: Main room
items: When the authors say trust is one of the most critical elements of AI adoption, what do they mean? Think of a tool you stopped trusting. What broke the trust?
Can anyone describe what happened between Google DeepMind and the Royal Free? Who do you think owns patient data, the patient, the doctor or the hospital, and what does the law say?

The authors say adoption must be considered from the moment a system is conceived until it is implemented and sustained. What examples do they give? Who should sit on the governance group that oversees it, and how do the authors think AI governance and regulation should work?

w1.label: If time allows
items: The authors call fairness, explainability and ethics the centre of the barriers. Are these what actually stops tools on the ground, or what papers like to write about?
Which barrier have you seen yourself, and which facilitator have you seen work?

w3.label: Breakout
items: Table 6 gives an odds ratio of 112 with no upper limit. What does that tell us, and how should we quote it?
The outcome is binary, success or not. What does that hide?
There were 71 comparisons and 18 variables. How much should we trust the four features?

w3.label: Main room
items: Then and now. These systems date from before 2003. Which of the four features still apply to AI tools today?
Involvement. Local user involvement did not predict success here, yet Sendak relied on it. Who is right?
MSK. Does a fracture detection tool meet the four features?

w16.label: Warm-up, quick answers from the reading set
items: Pick one review. What question did it ask, and what did it count as 'implementation'?
Which specialties already have a review of AI barriers and facilitators? Which one is missing?
What did the two deployed MSK tools, the theatre scheduling tool and the spine tools, actually change in practice?

w16.label: Round 1, breakout rooms, ideas from the papers (each room picks one)
items: Room 1. The theatre scheduling tool raised theatre efficiency from 39% to 93%. Why might a non-clinical tool be easier to deploy than a diagnostic one?
Room 2. Hogg 2023 used NASSS and the sepsis review used SALIENT. What does each framework notice that the other misses?
Room 3. Imaging, primary care and sepsis all have barrier reviews, but MSK care does not. Why do you think MSK has been left out?

w16.label: Round 1, main room
items: What was the most interesting or surprising point in the paper you read?
Was there a barrier or facilitator that appeared in almost every specialty? Is it really universal, or just the easiest one to measure?
What evidence would convince you that an AI tool is really used in routine care, and not only tested?

w16.label: Round 2, breakout rooms, back to our review (each room picks one)
items: Room 1, gap statement. Pick two reviews from table 1 and write one sentence each on how our review will be different. Together these become our gap statement.
Room 2, framework. Should we chart our studies with NASSS, SALIENT or both? What should we borrow, and what would not work for MSK care?
Room 3, screening rule. Does the theatre scheduling tool count as 'used in real-world MSK care'? Write a rule we can all apply at screening.

w16.label: Round 2, main room
items: List three things we will do the same as these reviews, and three things we will deliberately do differently.
Several reviews only judged AI by accuracy, or described their methods vaguely. How do we avoid repeating these weaknesses?
The James Lind Alliance lists the challenges of using digital tools in T&O as a top 10 research priority. How should we use this in our protocol and paper?
Which barrier do you expect to find in MSK care that the general reviews would miss?

w17.label: Warm-up, quick answers from the paper
items: What are the six barrier themes, and which theme had the most papers behind it?
Who wrote this review, and how might a team of NHS clinicians see barriers differently from engineers or managers?
The authors set their themes before reading the papers. How did they do this, and where did the themes come from?

w17.label: Round 1, breakout rooms, ideas from the paper (each room picks one)
items: Room 1. Most of the evidence in this review is opinion, not studies of real deployments. Does a barrier count if nobody has measured it?
Room 2. Liability and regulation is one theme. If an AI tool misses a fracture, who should be responsible, the clinician, the hospital or the company?
Room 3. Pick one theme, for example workforce or patient safety, and give a real example from your own work or training.

w17.label: Round 1, main room
items: This review lists barriers only, and Hassan 2024 in W1 looked at facilitators as well. What do we lose when a review leaves out facilitators?
Which of the six themes do you think matters most in the NHS today, and why?

w17.label: Round 2, breakout rooms, back to our review (each room picks one)
items: Room 1, themes. Should we start our charting with fixed themes, like Ahmed, or let themes come from the studies? What are the risks of each?
Room 2, evidence. Our review only includes tools used in practice. Write one rule that stops opinion pieces getting into our review.
Room 3, MSK. Go through the six themes. Which would look different in MSK care, and is any MSK barrier missing from the list?

w17.label: Round 2, main room
items: What is one thing we should learn from this review, and one thing we should not copy?
Can we use Ahmed's six themes as a checklist when we chart our studies? What would we need to add?
